intro/hello: This lecture is about scale, and about one surprisingly simple pattern.
intro/y2016: In 2016, making a network bigger was a gamble: nobody could say in advance how much better it would get.
intro/y2020: By 2020 that had changed. Train language models of different sizes, plot their loss on the right axes, and the points fall on a straight line.
intro/extend: And a straight line can be extended. You could predict how good a model would be before paying to train it.
intro/question: That turned scale into a research question. If you can afford a fixed amount of compute, how big should the model be, and how many tokens should it read?
intro/symbols: We will call the number of parameters N, the number of training tokens D, and the training compute C.
intro/loss: The loss is next-token cross-entropy, in nats. Lower is better.
intro/plan: We will build the answer in steps: power laws, fitting, counting compute, and two papers that answered very differently.
intro/go: Start with the shape of the curve itself.
power/def: A power law says y equals a, times x to the power minus k. Read x as model size, y as the loss, and k as a small positive number.
power/prop: Its defining property: multiply x by ten, and y gets multiplied by the same factor, wherever you start.
power/ex: With k equal to one half, every ten times more x leaves about a third of the y, from ten to a hundred, and from a hundred to a thousand.
power/plain: On ordinary axes that is hard to see. The curve drops fast, then crawls along a long, flat looking tail.
power/log: So switch both axes to a log scale, where every step is a power of ten.
power/straight: Now the curve is a straight line.
power/why: Taking logs turns the power into a multiplication: log y equals log a, minus k times log x. That is the equation of a straight line.
power/slope: And its slope is minus k. The exponent is literally the steepness of the line on log-log axes.
power/expo: Compare an exponential decay. It loses a fixed fraction per fixed step, not per fixed ratio, so on these axes it falls off a cliff.
fit/runs: Real experiments give noisy points. Here are ten small training runs, from a million to a billion parameters: synthetic, made up for this lecture.
fit/logs: Take the logarithm of each size and each loss.
fit/fit: Then fit a straight line by least squares, which makes the squared misses as small as possible. Its slope is the exponent.
fit/good: The line fits beautifully. So extend it a hundred times further, to a hundred billion parameters.
fit/miss: And the prediction is badly wrong. The true loss is much higher than the line says.
fit/floor: The reason is a floor. Language is partly unpredictable, so even a perfect model still pays some loss. Call that floor E.
fit/form: The honest law is a power law sitting on a floor: E, plus a times N to the minus k.
fit/narrow: Over a narrow range the floor is invisible. Extrapolate far, and the straight line dives right through it.
fit/refit: Fit the floor as well, and the curve bends. Now the prediction lands near the truth.
fit/gpt4: This is how big runs are planned. The GPT-4 report describes predicting its final loss from runs using up to ten thousand times less compute.
kaplan/paper: In January 2020, Jared Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI trained many transformer language models, up to one and a half billion parameters.
kaplan/three: They found three straight lines: loss against parameters, against data, and against compute. Each held while the other two were not the bottleneck.
kaplan/n: For parameters, the exponent was about zero point zero seven six.
kaplan/d: For data, about zero point zero nine five. And for compute, spent well, about zero point zero five.
kaplan/small: Those are small numbers. Doubling the parameters cuts the loss by only about five percent; ten times, by about sixteen.
kaplan/shape: Three more findings. Shape barely mattered: at a fixed parameter count, depth versus width hardly changed the loss.
kaplan/sample: Bigger models were more sample efficient: they reached a given loss after fewer tokens.
kaplan/together: And parameters and data have to grow together.
kaplan/bend: Fix the dataset and keep growing the model: the loss follows the line for a while, then bends flat. Data has become the bottleneck.
kaplan/slide: Give it more data, and the bend moves out to bigger models.
flops/flop: To use the compute law, we count compute in FLOPs: one multiply, or one add. Nearly all of it is matrix multiplies against the weights.
flops/fwd: In the forward pass, each weight multiplies one incoming number and adds the product into a sum. That is two FLOPs, per weight, per token.
flops/bx: Backpropagation needs two more products of the same size. One sends the gradient back to the layer's input: two more FLOPs.
flops/bw: The other computes the gradient of the weights themselves: two more.
flops/six: Six FLOPs per parameter, per token. So training costs about six, times N, times D.
flops/infer: Running a trained model is forward only: about two N per token. That number comes back at the end.
flops/gpt: GPT-3 had one hundred seventy five billion parameters and trained on three hundred billion tokens. Six times those is about three times ten to the twenty three FLOPs.
flops/days: At four hundred trillion FLOPs per second, that is about nine thousand GPU days, or nine days on a thousand GPUs.
flops/same: A curious fact: four famous models, G P T three, Gopher, Chinchilla, and Llama three with eight billion parameters, all used similar compute, within a factor of two and a half.
flops/split: They just split it very differently between parameters and tokens. That split is what the rest of this lecture is about.
frontier/one: Pick one model size and train it on more and more tokens. Each token costs six N FLOPs and lowers the loss, quickly at first, then slowly.
frontier/flat: Eventually the model's own size is the bottleneck, and its curve goes flat.
frontier/many: Now do that for many sizes, and plot every curve against compute.
frontier/cross: Small models are cheap per token, so they win at small budgets. Big models win at big budgets.
frontier/env: The lower edge of the whole family is the best loss any model can reach at each budget. That edge is the compute frontier.
frontier/straight: Subtract the floor, and the frontier is a straight line on log-log axes. That is Kaplan's law for compute.
frontier/move: As the budget grows, the winning size moves to the right.
frontier/kaplan: Kaplan measured how fast. The best model size grew as compute to the power zero point seven three, and the data only as the power zero point two seven.
frontier/tenx: Ten times more compute: a model about five times bigger, trained on fewer than twice as many tokens.
frontier/race: The field followed. GPT-3 put one hundred seventy five billion parameters on three hundred billion tokens. Gopher put two hundred eighty billion on the same tokens.
frontier/params: Megatron-Turing went to five hundred thirty billion, on even fewer. The race was for parameters; the tokens barely moved.
chinchilla/paper: In 2022, Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind asked the budget question again, more carefully.
chinchilla/runs: They trained over four hundred models, from seventy million to over sixteen billion parameters, on five to five hundred billion tokens.
chinchilla/sched: And they gave every run a learning rate schedule matched to its own length. That detail will matter.
chinchilla/three: They estimated the best split three independent ways. All three agreed with each other, and disagreed with Kaplan.
chinchilla/formula: The third way fits one formula for the loss in terms of both N and D.
chinchilla/e: First, a floor, E: the uncertainty left in text itself, which even a perfect model pays.
chinchilla/a: Plus a penalty for having only N parameters: A over N to the alpha. It shrinks as the model grows.
chinchilla/b: Plus a penalty for having seen only D tokens: B over D to the beta. It shrinks with more data.
chinchilla/exps: Their fit put alpha and beta both near zero point three.
chinchilla/neither: Each penalty falls by a fixed fraction for every ten times more of its resource, and neither reaches zero. A fixed budget means buying some of each.
chinchilla/approx: Treat the constants as approximate; a later replication re-estimated them. The pictures use round illustrative numbers of the same form.
budget/plane: Draw a map. Model size runs across, tokens run up, and both axes are logarithmic.
budget/contours: The loss formula draws contours on this map: lines of equal loss, like height lines on a hiking map. Lower loss is up and to the right.
budget/line: Now fix a budget. Every way to spend it all satisfies C equals six N D, and on these axes that is a straight line, sloping down.
budget/walk: Walk along the line. Far left, the model is tiny and starved for capacity. Far right, it is huge and starved for data.
budget/valley: Plot the loss as you walk, and you get a valley.
budget/touch: The bottom of the valley is where the budget line just touches the lowest contour it can reach.
budget/answer: For Chinchilla's budget, about six times ten to the twenty three FLOPs, the bottom is near seventy billion parameters and one point four trillion tokens.
budget/gpt3: GPT-3's split, under two tokens per parameter, sits up the right slope of the same valley: a worse loss for the same money.
budget/grow: Now increase the budget. The line slides outward, and the best point slides with it.
budget/diag: And it slides along a straight diagonal: about twenty tokens for every parameter, at every budget.
twenty/why: Why a fixed ratio? Do the calculus at the bottom of the valley, and the best size grows as compute to the power beta, over alpha plus beta.
twenty/data: The tokens get the rest: alpha over alpha plus beta. The two shares add up to one.
twenty/equal: When the two penalties shrink at the same rate, both shares are one half.
twenty/tenx: Then ten times more compute buys about three times more parameters and three times more tokens.
twenty/kaplan: Chinchilla's three methods put the size exponent between zero point four six and one half. Kaplan had zero point seven three.
twenty/under: By this measure, the giant models of 2020 and 2021 were badly undertrained: too many parameters, too few tokens.
twenty/test: DeepMind tested it directly. Chinchilla: seventy billion parameters, trained on one point four trillion tokens, with about the same compute as Gopher.
twenty/gopher: Gopher had four times the parameters, and under a quarter of the data. Same area, different shape.
twenty/won: Chinchilla beat Gopher on the large majority of tasks, and at a quarter of the size, it was much cheaper to run.
twenty/whyk: Why did Kaplan differ? The Chinchilla paper pointed mainly at the learning rate schedule.
twenty/sched: Kaplan used one schedule length no matter when a run would stop, so short runs were measured before their learning rate came down. That made short training look worse.
twenty/lesson: The lesson: a scaling law is a fact about a training recipe. Change a careless detail, and the law tilts.
beyond/once: Chinchilla answers one question exactly: the cheapest way to train a model to a given loss.
beyond/used: But a model is trained once and then used, often by many people, for a long time.
beyond/serve: Every token it processes costs about two N FLOPs. A smaller model is cheaper for every one of them, and faster too.
beyond/trade: And a smaller model can still reach the same loss by reading more tokens, because the data penalty keeps shrinking.
beyond/curve: So hold the loss fixed and slide toward smaller models. Training compute rises, because each one needs more tokens.
beyond/serveline: Serving compute falls in proportion to size.
beyond/best: The best size balances the two.
beyond/more: Now let it serve more and more tokens. The best size moves left, and its tokens per parameter climb into the hundreds, then thousands.
beyond/llama: That is what happened. Meta's first LLaMA trained a seven billion parameter model on a trillion tokens.
beyond/llama3: Llama 3 trained an eight billion parameter model on over fifteen trillion tokens, about seventy five times the Chinchilla optimal amount, and it kept improving.
beyond/least: Chinchilla optimal became the least data a serious model is trained on, not the target.
limits/one: A scaling law predicts one number, the average loss, for one recipe. A few caveats keep it in its place.
limits/ability: First, loss is not ability. The loss falls smoothly, but a specific skill can seem to appear suddenly.
limits/exact: Suppose each token of a twenty token answer is right with probability p, and the answer counts only if all are right: the score is p to the twentieth.
limits/jump: As p climbs smoothly from one half to zero point nine five, the score leaps from one in a million to about a third.
limits/emerge: Jumps like this were called emergent abilities. Many of them turn smooth when measured with a continuous score.
limits/data: Second, data is finite. Repeating data for up to about four epochs is nearly as good as fresh, and then the returns fall away.
limits/recipe: Third, the constants belong to a recipe. Better data, architecture, or optimizer moves the whole line down.
limits/other: And training is not the only axis: spending more compute at inference, by thinking longer, has its own curve, later in the course.
outro/line: Let's recap. On log-log axes a power law is a straight line, and its slope is the exponent. Fit it on the logs, and remember the floor.
outro/laws: Loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute, as long as none of them is the bottleneck.
outro/six: Training costs about six N D FLOPs. Running the model costs about two N per token.
outro/twenty: For a fixed budget, grow the model and the data together: about twenty tokens per parameter.
outro/longer: And if the model will be used a lot, make it smaller, and train it much longer.
outro/next: In the interactive chapter you can fit these lines yourself, slide a compute budget, and size a model for its users.
